# Finding black hole spins efficiently during a numerical binary evolution

**Authors:** Himanshu Chaudhary1,∗ Rob Owen2 Mark A. Scheel1 and Saul A. Teukolsky1,3 Affiliation: 1Theoretical Astrophysics 350-17, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, 91125, USA Affiliation: 2Department of Physics and Astronomy, Oberlin College Affiliation: 3Cornell Center for Astrophysics and Planetary Science, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14853, USA Affiliation: ∗Author to whom any correspondence should be addressed. Email: hchaudha@caltech.edu

## Abstract

The dynamics of a binary black hole system depend on its masses and spins. For a binary at finite separation, it is not possible to define these quantities in an unambiguous way; however, there are several reasonable definitions that reduce to the expected values in the limit of infinite separation. Approximate Killing vector (AKV) spin is one of the spin definitions used in the numerical relativity code SpEC. AKV spin requires finding approximate Killing vectors on an apparent horizon, which reduces to a generalized eigenvalue problem of size $\mathcal{O}(L^{2})$ , and a direct solve has time complexity $\mathcal{O}(L^{6})$ , where $L$ is the highest spherical harmonic mode used to represent the apparent horizon. This scaling means that the cost of computing AKV spins increases rapidly as we simulate systems at higher resolutions, especially those with high spin or mass ratios. We describe a new algorithm for computing AKV spins that is much faster than the current algorithm.

#### keywords

## 1 Introduction

Detectors in the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) [1, 2] collaboration require accurate gravitational-wave models to detect and analyze signals from binary black hole (BBH) mergers [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. The only first-principles way to produce gravitational-wave models for the full inspiral, merger, and ringdown is numerical relativity (NR) [8, 9, 10], which solves Einstein’s equations directly on a computer. NR simulations are very expensive and slow, which limits their direct use for data analysis. Instead, NR simulations are used as a source of ground truth to construct and calibrate other models like surrogate models [11, 12, 13, 14, 15] and Effective-One-Body (EOB) models [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21], which are then used for detection and data analysis. Until now, the accuracy of Numerical Relativity (NR) simulations has been sufficient for the gravitational-wave detections made by the LVK collaboration. However, with the new generation of gravitational-wave detectors coming online [22, 23, 24], many NR simulations will need to be redone at higher resolution to keep the NR error negligible in data analysis [25].

In NR, the masses and spins of black holes are not input parameters, but instead they are time-dependent output parameters that are measured from the numerical solution of Einstein’s equations. In practice, achieving some chosen masses and spins even at the initial time of the simulation involves guessing “bare” masses and spins, solving the Einstein constraint equations, measuring the masses and spins, adjusting the bare values, and iterating until the measured values match the desired ones [26].

When running the code SpEC [27] for binary black hole (BBH) simulations at high resolution, we noticed a dramatic slowdown that we ultimately traced to the algorithm that computes the spin of each dynamical black hole. This algorithm, which computes the approximate Killing vector (AKV) spin [28, 29], involves solving a generalized eigenvalue problem on an apparent horizon. The apparent horizon is represented as a surface of angularly dependent coordinate radius $r_{\mathrm{AH}}(\theta,\phi)=\sum_{\ell,m}S_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi)$ , where $Y_{\ell m}$ are spherical harmonics, $S_{\ell m}$ are coefficients, and the sum goes up to some value $L$ that depends on the resolution. The reason for the slowdown is that the AKV eigenvalue problem involves a matrix of size $L^{2}\times L^{2}$ , and for high resolution, $L$ can grow to 100 or more, especially for large spins or extreme mass ratios. The AKV calculation is performed on a single core, since it was (incorrectly) assumed to be a small computational cost compared to the remainder of the BBH evolution.

The outline of this paper is as follows. Section 2 has some mathematical background about how the AKV spins are defined. Then, in Section 3, we briefly describe the existing algorithm and why it slows down rapidly as the systems being evolved get complicated. In Section 4, we describe the new algorithm, which is much faster. Finally, we discuss possible future improvements in Section 5 and present conclusions in Section 6.

## 2 AKV spin definition

In this section, we only briefly describe the algorithm. The reader should refer to Appendix A of [28] and Ref. [29] for more background and references.

There is no unambiguous way to define the spin of a dynamical black hole horizon in a BBH system. We usually compute a quasilocal spin definition that reduces to the expected well-defined value in the limit of infinite separation. AKV spin is one of these quasilocal spin definitions, constructed using approximate Killing vectors of the black hole horizons.

We start by setting up the conventions used throughout the paper. We work in the standard 3+1 decomposition [8, 9, 10], with the spatial slice denoted by $\Sigma$ . The spatial metric, extrinsic curvature, and the two-dimensional apparent horizon are denoted by $g_{ij}$ , $K_{ij}$ , and $\mathcal{H}$ , respectively. Lower-case Latin letters index the spatial tensors, and upper-case Latin letters index the tensors on the two-dimensional horizon surface. We also put a circle above the geometric quantities related to $\mathcal{H}$ to separate them from the geometric quantities on the spatial slice $\Sigma$ .

In NR, the standard definition [30] of spin angular momentum is given by

$$ \displaystyle S=\frac{1}{8\pi}\oint_{\mathcal{H}}\phi^{i}s^{j}K_{ij}dA $$

where $s^{j}$ is the outgoing unit normal to $\mathcal{H}$ . Here $\vec{\phi}$ is an “azimuthal” vector field, tangent to $\mathcal{H}$ , which carries the information about the spin axis.

It can be shown that Eq.(1) is conserved [30] when $\vec{\phi}$ is a Killing vector of the dynamical horizon world tube. For an isolated Kerr black hole, this Killing vector defines the spin axis of the horizon, but there is no reason why such a Killing vector field should exist for the horizon of a black hole in a binary system. The next best thing one can use is the vector field that is closest to being a Killing vector field; in other words, an approximate Killing vector. We now describe the method used in SpEC to construct these approximate Killing vector fields. We start from Killing’s equation for a vector field $\phi_{B}$

$$ \displaystyle D_{(A}\phi_{B)}=0, $$

where $D$ is the covariant derivative compatible with the metric $\mathring{g}_{AB}$ on the two-dimensional horizon surface. This condition can be split into two conditions: first, that the field has no divergence

$$ \displaystyle\Theta:=\mathring{g}^{AB}D_{A}\phi_{B}=0, $$

where $\mathring{g}_{AB}$ is the metric on the horizon surface. The second condition is that the field has no shear

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{AB}:=D_{(A}\phi_{B)}-\frac{1}{2}\mathring{g}_{AB}\Theta=0. $$

If $\vec{\phi}$ is not a Killing vector field, we cannot satisfy both conditions simultaneously, so we will choose a $\vec{\phi}$ that is divergence-free and has the smallest possible shear. Any divergence-free vector field tangent to the apparent horizon can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\phi^{A}=\epsilon^{AB}D_{B}z, $$

where $z$ is some smooth function and $\epsilon^{AB}$ is the Levi-Civita tensor. The problem of finding the approximate Killing vector then reduces to finding the $z$ that gives the smallest shear, or equivalently, minimizes the norm $\|\sigma\|^{2}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\|\sigma\|^{2}:=\oint_{\mathcal{H}}\sigma_{BC}\sigma^{BC}dA. $$

Using Eqs.(4) and (5) and integrating by parts, we get

$$ \displaystyle\|\sigma\|^{2}=\oint_{\mathcal{H}}zHzdA. $$

Here $H$ is

$$ \displaystyle Hz=D^{4}z+\mathring{R}D^{2}z+(D^{A}\mathring{R})(D_{A}z) $$

where $D^{2}$ is the Laplacian on the apparent horizon and $\mathring{R}$ is the Ricci scalar. If we minimize Eq.(7) with respect to $z$ , we obtain the trivial solution where $z$ is constant and $\vec{\phi}$ is zero. To avoid this, we will require that the minimized $\vec{\phi}$ has a positive norm,

$$ \displaystyle\oint_{\mathcal{H}}\phi^{A}\phi_{A}dA>0 $$

Using a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$ and the fact that $\phi^{A}\phi_{A}=D^{A}zD_{A}z$ , we get

$$ \displaystyle I[z]:=\oint_{\mathcal{H}}zHzdA+\lambda\left(\oint_{\mathcal{H}}D^{A}zD_{A}zdA-\mathcal{N}\right), $$

where $\mathcal{N}$ is a still-undetermined positive constant. Fixing the value of $\mathcal{N}$ is equivalent to normalizing the approximate Killing vector field, which determines both the spin axis and the spin magnitude.

Minimizing the functional (10) with respect to $z$ gives a generalized eigenvalue problem:

$$ \displaystyle Hz=\lambda D^{2}z $$

We can try to discretize Eq.(11) and solve it numerically. The only remaining issue is that both $H$ and $D^{2}$ still share a kernel in which $z$ is constant, making this eigenvalue problem singular. The standard way to deal with such issues is to remove the common kernel space and then solve for $z$ . In our case, this is trivial because we are discretizing using spherical harmonics and can just remove the $Y_{00}$ mode.

On a metrically round two-sphere, the scalar potentials associated with rotational Killing vector fields are the three $\ell=1$ spherical harmonics. After removing the constant $Y_{00}$ mode, we therefore retain the three least-shear eigenvectors, which provide a natural generalization of this three-dimensional rotation subspace to a deformed horizon. Although only the first eigenvector strictly minimizes the shear, the three least-shear eigenvectors together define the preferred subspace of generalized rotation generators.

From Eq. (7) and Eq. (11), we can see that the amount of shear is proportional to the magnitude of $\lambda$ . Therefore, once we have discretized Eq. (11), the next step is to find the three smallest-magnitude eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenfunctions. We can use these eigenfunctions $z$ to compute the components of the spin along the corresponding axes. However, we still need to determine the spin magnitude by normalizing the eigenfunctions, which is equivalent to fixing $\mathcal{N}$ in Eq. (10). To fix this normalization, we use

$$ \displaystyle\oint_{\mathcal{H}}(z-\langle\langle z\rangle\rangle)^{2}dA=\frac{A^{3}}{48\pi^{2}} $$

where $\langle\langle z\rangle\rangle$ is the average of $z$ over the surface and $A$ is the surface area of the apparent horizon. We use this equation to normalize the three eigenfunctions, after which their Euclidean norms give the spin magnitude. Mathematically, Eq. (12) holds only for a Kerr metric, where $z$ is a true rotation generator of the horizon. Therefore, when using it for normalization, we assume that the evolving black holes are approximately Kerr.

Using the AKV potential $z$ and the normalization condition in Eq.(12) is the most robust way we know to get the spin magnitude, and it is what we use by default in SpEC. Determining the spin axis is much more complicated, and not all definitions are based on $z$ . Various definitions of the spin axis, along with their trade-offs, are discussed in [29].

Now that we have some understanding of why we need to solve a generalized eigenvalue problem, we next describe the current algorithm and explain why it becomes problematic for complex systems.

## 3 Current AKV algorithm

Call the matrices formed by discretizing the operators $H$ and $D^{2}$ in Eq.(11) $M$ and $B$ , respectively. Now we have a generalized eigenvalue problem $Mx=\lambda Bx$ , and the obvious way to obtain the eigenvectors is to use a standard library such as LAPACK [31]. To understand why this becomes an issue, we need to understand how big these matrices are and how they grow with an increase in the complexity of the apparent horizons.

Apparent horizons in SpEC are represented using spherical harmonics. When the black holes are far away from each other, their apparent horizons are mostly spherical and can be approximated using a small number of spherical harmonics. On the other hand, when the black holes are about to merge, the horizons become very distorted, and we need a larger number of spherical harmonics to approximate them. We will denote the highest spherical harmonic used in representing the apparent horizon as $L$ . For the simulations that we have done so far, $L$ can be as small as 15 during the inspiral, but in some complex cases it can get as large as 90 near the merger. As we push to evolve more and more complex systems at higher and higher resolution, we expect the largest required value of $L$ to increase even further.

*Figure 1: Scaling of various parts of the algorithm with the highest spherical harmonic mode $L$ . The runs were performed on Caltech HPC (Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8276 CPU @ 2.20GHz). The solid dots are the real data, while the dotted lines show the best fits. The fits were weighted such that the measurements at higher $L$ have more weight, as they are less noisy. The legends include the scaling from these fits. We see that the scalings of matrix generation and dggev are slightly worse than the theoretical expectations of $\mathcal{O}(L^{4})$ and $\mathcal{O}(L^{6})$ , respectively. Note that the new AKV algorithm using ARPACK + LU decomposition (purple + black lines) is orders of magnitude faster than the current AKV algorithm using dggev (blue line). By a large margin, the current bottleneck is matrix generation (red line).*

The number of rows in the $M$ and $B$ matrices is $N=(L-1)^{2}-1$ . The reason for $L-1$ is that even though we have $L+1$ modes, we take second derivatives, and that pollutes the two highest modes. The term $-1$ is because we ignore $Y_{00}$ , as described in Sec.(2). We only need the eigenvectors corresponding to the three smallest-magnitude eigenvalues, but using LAPACK’s dense solver (dggev) means we always compute all eigenvalues ( $L^{2}$ in number)11 1 There are other LAPACK routines that can select the three required eigenvalues and compute only their eigenvectors, but they provide very little speedup [31, Sec. 3.4.3]. Before finding the eigenvectors, LAPACK performs an eigensystem reduction, which is the most costly operation. Once the reduction is done, finding the eigenvectors themselves is comparatively cheap, which means that finding just a few eigenvectors is not significantly faster than finding all of them.. The theoretical time complexity of LAPACK’s dggev solver is $\mathcal{O}(N^{3})$ , or equivalently $\mathcal{O}(L^{6})$ . This is the reason why the cost of dggev is irrelevant for most of the inspiral until we get close to merger, where it starts to increase rapidly. In our simulations, we have found the scaling to be closer to $\mathcal{O}(L^{7})$ , as shown in Figs. (1) and (4). We suspect that the slightly worse scaling may be due to memory pressure since the matrix has $\mathcal{O}(L^{4})$ elements, although we have not rigorously verified this.

From Table (1), we see that the runtime cost of dggev goes from $0.07$ s to $13{,}100$ s as $L$ goes from 15 to 100. For some simulations, each such spin calculation took over 30 minutes on a single core, tying up that core while the rest of the cores wasted resources waiting for it to finish. This waste of computing resources would only get worse with the need to run more accurate simulations. In the next section, we outline a new algorithm that uses the iterative eigensolver ARPACK to efficiently compute the three required eigenvectors, providing a large speedup.

## 4 ARPACK-based AKV algorithm

From the previous Section 3, we saw that the primary cause of the poor scaling of the current AKV algorithm is the LAPACK routine dggev, which solves for the whole eigensystem. To find the AKV spin, we only require the three smallest-magnitude eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors. There are standard iterative algorithms, implemented in libraries like ARPACK [32], that can find just the required eigenpairs very efficiently. For a highly deformed horizon, where $L\approx 100$ , dggev finds all $\approx 10^{4}$ eigenpairs, and we can significantly reduce the required computation by finding only the three required eigenpairs using ARPACK. To find an eigenpair, ARPACK just needs a series of matrix-vector products until it converges to the required solution. Because we only need three eigenpairs, the theoretical computational complexity of using ARPACK is $\mathcal{O}(L^{4})$ , which is much better than that of dggev ( $\mathcal{O}(L^{6})$ ).

In the following sections, we will first discuss issues that ARPACK has in trying to find the eigenvalues with very small magnitude and how to resolve them. Then we will discuss the cost of assembling the matrices $M$ and $B$ . Finally, we will discuss the cost of getting the action of the inverse of these matrices required by ARPACK.

### 4.1 Shift-invert transform

The number of iterations needed by ARPACK to converge depends on the distribution of the eigenvalues. If we are trying to find the first few largest-magnitude eigenvalues and they are well separated, then the convergence is very fast. On the other hand, if we are trying to find the smallest-magnitude eigenvalues, convergence is very slow, and it might not even converge for some systems. For problems like ours, where we need to find the smallest-magnitude eigenvalues, the way to maintain good convergence is to use the shift-invert transform.

The shift-invert transform is a method for transforming our eigenvalue problem into another in which the desired eigenvalues become large in magnitude and well separated from their neighbors. The original problem is

$$ Mx=\lambda Bx $$

After applying the shift-invert transform, it becomes:

$$ (M-\sigma B)^{-1}Bx=\nu x, $$

where $\sigma$ is a free parameter we can choose, and

$$ \nu=\frac{1}{\lambda-\sigma}. $$

The first thing to observe is that both problems have the same eigenvectors, while the corresponding eigenvalues are related by Eq.(15). From Eq.(15), we see that among the new eigenvalues in Eq. (14), $|\nu|$ is largest for the values of $\lambda$ that are closest to $\sigma$ . So if we want to find the three smallest-magnitude eigenvalues, we should just set $\sigma=0$ and ask ARPACK for the largest-magnitude transformed eigenvalues. This will work until one of the eigenvalues gets too close to $\sigma$ , and then the condition number of the matrix $M-\sigma B$ will diverge. One could consider shifting the value of $\sigma$ slightly away from zero, but then we would find the three eigenvalues closest to $\sigma$ , not the three smallest-magnitude eigenvalues.

This is not an issue if we are finding these eigenvectors in isolation, because we can always adjust the value of $\sigma$ slightly and then try again. In a long-running simulation where the eigenvalues keep changing, we cannot afford to suddenly have slightly wrong eigenvectors because one of the eigenvalues drifts too close to the value of $\sigma$ . Fortunately, since we are using the norm described in Eq.(9), the matrices $M$ and $B$ are positive- and negative-semidefinite, respectively, which implies that the generalized eigenvalues $\lambda$ are non-positive. Thus, any positive value of $\sigma$ will always give us the correct results. If we choose a small value of $\sigma$ , the eigenvalues we need will be well separated and large in magnitude, making ARPACK very efficient at finding them. But we do not want $\sigma$ to be too small because that makes the matrix $M-\sigma B$ ill-conditioned. This means that there is an ideal value of $\sigma$ that makes the magnitude of the transformed eigenvalues corresponding to the smallest-magnitude eigenvalues as large as possible, without making the matrix $M-\sigma B$ too ill-conditioned. Figs.(3(a)) and (3(b)) show how the condition number of $(M-\sigma B)$ and the number of iterations taken by ARPACK depend on $\sigma$ . For these two figures, $M$ and $B$ were generated using the horizon of a Kerr-Schild metric with spin $(0,0,0.5)$ and a mass of 1. These figures change for different shapes of the apparent horizons, but the same overall trend is always present.

For the systems that we tested, the eigenvalues found by ARPACK were very accurate even for very small values of $\sigma$ for which the condition number became as large as $10^{12}$ . In fact, for large values of $L$ , the eigenvalues found by ARPACK were more accurate than those found by dggev, especially when one of the eigenvalues was very close to zero. In practice, the accuracy of the eigenvalues found by either solver is adequate for our purposes because we are limited by errors in other parts of the algorithm, such as finding the apparent horizons. For now, we have decided to choose $\sigma=0.1$ as the default value for our simulations, which allows for rapid convergence without generating very ill-conditioned matrices. Note that not all norms lead to eigenvalue problems in which all eigenvalues are negative. For example, the norm used by Cook and Whiting [33] will not have this property, making it hard to choose a stable and effective value for $\sigma$ .

### 4.2 Cost of assembling the matrices

Recall that matrices $M$ and $B$ represent the discretization of the operators $H$ and $D^{2}$ that appear in Eq.(11). It is not straightforward to derive explicit formulas for $M$ and $B$ , but SpEC has two functions, $f_{M}(x)$ and $f_{B}(x)$ , that give the action of the matrices $M$ and $B$ on a vector $x$ . To generate the matrices, we need to operate on $N$ Cartesian basis vectors, which can be costly.

It is important to consider the cost of the matrix generation because, in theory, we do not even need to construct these matrices when using ARPACK. From Table (1), we see that the cost of constructing the matrix exceeds that of dggev for $L<25$ . We expect the time complexity of generating the matrices $M$ and $B$ to be around $\mathcal{O}(N^{2})$ : one factor of $N$ arises because we need to act on $N$ basis vectors, and another because the cost of the functions $f_{M}(x)$ and $f_{B}(x)$ is $\mathcal{O}(N)$ . From Figs. (1) and (4), we see that the cost lies between $\mathcal{O}(L^{4.5})$ and $\mathcal{O}(L^{5})$ depending on the system we are running on. This scaling behavior means that the cost of dggev quickly overtakes the cost of constructing the matrices, becoming the main bottleneck.

Like many iterative algorithms, ARPACK can work directly with the functions $f_{M}(x)$ and $f_{B}(x)$ , saving both memory and computation. Working in this matrix-free manner was our original plan, but it failed for reasons described in detail in Appendix (B). The final version we ended up using involves constructing the full matrices $M$ and $B$ , and we will assume that we have access to those in the later sections.

### 4.3 Cost of $(M-\sigma B)^{-1}$

When ARPACK solves a sparse eigenvalue problem, for example $Mx=\lambda x$ , it does so iteratively. On each iteration, ARPACK provides a trial eigenvector $x$ to the user, the user code computes $Mx$ and sends it to ARPACK, and then ARPACK updates its trial eigenvector for the next iteration. Similarly, for the shift-invert system, ARPACK still provides a trial eigenvector $x$ to the user. The user code computes $(M-\sigma B)^{-1}Bx$ and sends it to ARPACK, which updates $x$ until convergence. A typical iteration of ARPACK solving a shift-invert system is shown in Fig.(2). Note that it requires us to solve the linear system $(M-\sigma B)y=Bx$ . For $\sigma=0.1$ , ARPACK usually needs around 30 iterations to get the three smallest-magnitude eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors. Of course, we do not want to take the inverse of the matrix explicitly, so two options are solving the linear system using LU decomposition or using iterative methods. For reasons mentioned in Appendix B, we will avoid iterative methods and focus on using LU decomposition to solve the linear system.

Now the theoretical issue with using LU decomposition is that it scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^{3})\approx\mathcal{O}(L^{6})$ , which is the same as dggev. This means that scaling-wise, we have just pushed the problem from dggev to the LU solve. But unlike dggev, LU factorization is much more optimized22 2 Part of the reason is that LU decomposition makes very good use of BLAS Level 3 routines while dggev does not. In general, the number of flops required for an LU decomposition is much smaller than that required by dggev. Thus, in practice, LU decomposition is much faster, even if both theoretically scale as $\mathcal{O}(N^{3})$ . and runs at least two orders of magnitude faster than dggev, as we can see from Table 1.

Of course, because of the $\mathcal{O}(L^{6})$ scaling for very large $L$ , the cost of LU decomposition will eventually overtake the cost of matrix generation. Extrapolating the measured scaling, for the systems we are solving this will happen only when $L\approx 10^{3}$ , well beyond our expected use cases.

Note that while ARPACK requires the actions of $(M-\sigma B)^{-1}$ for each iteration it takes, we only need to do the costly LU factorization once and then cache it. Getting the action of $(M-\sigma B)^{-1}$ on a vector from a cached LU factorization is almost as cheap as a simple matrix-vector product. From Table 1, we can see that the cost of doing the LU decomposition is negligible compared to the cost of constructing the matrices.

## 5 Future improvements

The first possible improvement to try is to get the matrix-free version of the algorithm working. The idea would be to generate the full matrices every 100th step or so to use as a preconditioner for the iterations. If the spin does not change very rapidly, then the matrix should also change slowly, and the same preconditioner could be used for multiple time steps. The main issue is that, close to the merger, spins change rapidly, and we may end up calculating the full matrices much more frequently.

Another possibility is to obtain a better preconditioner using the analytical properties of the matrices, which will allow us to work in a matrix-free manner, avoiding the cost of constructing the matrices $M$ and $B$ . The construction of the matrices requires $L^{2}$ calls to the functions $f_{M}$ and $f_{B}$ , which is the bottleneck in the new algorithm. When using a matrix-free version, we need to use an iterative linear solver like GMRES, which will call these functions multiple times to get the action of $(M-\sigma B)^{-1}$ . In our testing, we have found that with $\sigma=0.1$ , ARPACK typically requires fewer than 30 iterations to converge. For the matrix-free version to be faster, the total number of calls to $f_{M}$ and $f_{B}$ made by the ARPACK and linear-solver iterations needs to stay below the $N\sim L^{2}$ calls required to generate the full matrices, which is very hard to do without a good preconditioner.

Note that matrix generation is an embarrassingly parallel problem in which we apply the functions $f_{M}$ and $f_{B}$ to unit vectors one by one to construct the matrices. For large values of $L$ , we can gain a good speedup by doing this in parallel, especially for next-generation codes like SpECTRE [34] with better parallelism infrastructure than SpEC.

## 6 Conclusion

We have shown that the new algorithm based on the eigensystem solver (ARPACK) and LU decomposition is close to two orders of magnitude faster than the original one based on the dense eigensystem solver (LAPACK). If we include the time required to construct the matrices, which is required by both algorithms, then the speedup is closer to one order of magnitude. We tried to use a fully matrix-free algorithm, but were unable to find preconditioners for which the overall cost of the iterations and the preconditioner construction was lower than the cost of constructing the full matrix. However, the idea of using the fixed full matrix for a number of timesteps as a preconditioner is a promising future improvement to explore.

## Appendix B Matrix-free version of the AKV algorithm

*Figure 5: Matrix-free workflow for ARPACK in the generalized shift-invert case. Instead of explicitly forming $M$ and $B$ , we use the functions $f_{M}$ and $f_{B}$ , which are available in SpEC. At each iteration, ARPACK supplies a vector $x$ , and we solve $(f_{M}-\sigma f_{B})(y)=f_{B}(x)$ using an iterative solver. The result $y=(M-\sigma B)^{-1}Bx$ is returned to ARPACK for the next iteration.*

As already mentioned in section 4.2, the original goal was not to construct the matrices $M$ and $B$ at all but to use the functions $f_{M}$ and $f_{B}$ directly. This is shown in Fig.(5), where we skip the matrix construction and the LU decomposition.

We need to solve the linear problem $(f_{M}-\sigma f_{B})y=f_{B}(x)$ to get the vector $y$ required by ARPACK. This can be done using iterative solvers like GMRES or BiCGSTAB. In almost all cases, these iterative algorithms require a good preconditioner to converge at an acceptable rate. This is particularly true in our case because the condition number of the matrix $(M-\sigma B)$ is fairly big for $\sigma=0.1$ , and if we try to make $\sigma$ larger, then the number of iterations required by ARPACK increases significantly, as shown in Figs. 3(a) and 3(b). Note that we need the number of iterations required by ARPACK times the number of iterations required by the linear solver to stay below $N\sim L^{2}$ . Otherwise, the whole algorithm will be as costly as constructing the full matrix.

We tried a few simple preconditioners, and the algorithm worked very well most of the time. However, the convergence became very slow in some edge cases when the horizon was very deformed. Since the spin computation is ideally only a small part of a very large simulation, we would prefer a stable but slightly inefficient algorithm over a mostly stable but fast one. And while constructing the matrices is costly, using LU decomposition gives ARPACK robust convergence and predictable runtime even when the condition number gets large. Thus, we decided to swallow the cost of constructing the full matrices $M$ and $B$ and then use LU factorization to efficiently apply the action of $(M-\sigma B)^{-1}$ .

Using the matrix-free version in practice requires a good preconditioner that can be constructed cheaply. When there is no underlying structure and the matrices are dense, the standard methods for constructing non-trivial preconditioners from $f_{M}(x)$ are usually as costly as constructing the full matrix itself.

## Appendix C Speed difference between finding the smallest-magnitude and the largest-magnitude eigenvalues

ARPACK converges much faster when we solve for largest-magnitude eigenvalues that are well separated. We can see this if we generate a diagonal matrix with entries $1,4,9,16,\ldots,500^{2}$ and use ARPACK to find the eigenvalues. Finding the three smallest-magnitude eigenvalues requires 31302 matrix-vector products, while finding the three largest-magnitude eigenvalues only requires 430 matrix-vector products. This artificial example demonstrates the fact that ARPACK is more effective in finding the largest eigenvalues. If we use the shift-invert transform, which essentially transforms the smallest-magnitude eigenvalues into the largest-magnitude ones, ARPACK becomes much more efficient and requires only 38 inverse-operator applications to find the three smallest eigenvalues. This artificial example illustrates the importance of the shift-invert transform and the reduction in operator applications that can be achieved. In our case, for a black hole with spin $(0,0,0.5)$ , we use around 20 times fewer operator applications for $L=15$ and around 200 times fewer operator applications for $L=50$ , and the advantage of using shift-invert continues to increase as the matrix size grows.

## ABSTRACT

The nature of dark energy remains one of the most fundamental open questions in modern cosmology. Among the proposed extensions of the standard cosmological model, interacting dark energy scenarios provide a physically motivated framework for exploring possible energy exchange within the dark sector and the dynamical evolution of cosmic acceleration. In this work, we present a comprehensive observational study of the Interacting Metastable Emergent Dark Energy (IMEDE) model using the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Data Release 2 (DESI DR2) baryon acoustic oscillation measurements, together with Planck PR4 CamSpec cosmic microwave background observations and three independent Type Ia supernova compilations: Pantheon+, DES-Dovekie, and Union3. We ﬁnd that the IMEDE model provides a consistently better description of the DESI DR2 observations than the standard ΛCDM cosmology, with weak to moderate statistical signiﬁcance based on the best-ﬁt likelihood analysis and strong to decisive Bayesian evidence across the different dataset combinations. This statistical preference originates from a coherent reduction of the residuals across several independent BAO distance measurements rather than from any individual outlying data point. The reconstructed dark energy equation of state shows a transition from a phantom phase to a quintessence phase, crossing the phantom divide at z ≃0.3–0.5, characteristic of a Quintom-B dark energy scenario. Although the IMEDE model does not resolve the H0 or S8 tensions and provides no evidence for an interaction between dark matter and dark energy, it is well supported by the current cosmological data sets and motivates further tests with forthcoming DESI DR3 and next-generation cosmological surveys.

## Introduction

The Λ Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) model serves as the standard cosmological paradigm, providing a comprehensive description of large-scale structure, cosmic microwave background anisotropies, and the background expansion history of the Universe. This model assumes a spatially ﬂat geometry dominated by CDM and a cosmological constant (Λ), which drives the accelerated expansion observed at late times1–4. Despite its empirical success, the ΛCDM framework presents signiﬁcant theoretical difﬁculties and increasing observational inconsistencies5,6. Theoretically, the model is limited by the cosmological

constant problem, characterized by the extensive magnitude difference between the observed Λ value and the vacuum energy density predicted by quantum ﬁeld theory, which introduces a strict ﬁne-tuning requirement7–9. Another limitation is the coincidence problem, which concerns the comparable magnitudes of dark energy and dark matter densities strictly in the present epoch10,11. Observationally, the model shows discrepancies between early-universe predictions and late-time local measurements, speciﬁcally the Hubble (H0) tension and the structure growth (S8) tension12–17. These issues have motivated the development of alternative theoretical formulations, such as dynamical dark energy models18–22, interacting dark

sectors23–27, and modiﬁed theories of gravity28–33. The DESI DR2 provides new insights into the nature of dark energy34. When DESI DR2 is combined with CMB observations, the w0waCDM model favors a dynamical dark energy scenario over the ΛCDM model, characterized by the Quintom-B behavior (w0 > −1, wa < 0, and w0 +wa < −1)35. The inclusion of the Pantheon+, Union3, and DESY5 Type Ia supernova datasets further strengthens this preference, increasing the signiﬁcance to 2.8σ, 3.8σ, and 4.2σ, respectively. Later, the revised DESY5 dataset was recalibrated and released as DES-Dovekie36. Using this updated supernova compilation, the preference for dynamical dark energy remains signiﬁcant at 3.2σ, although it is reduced compared to the 4.2σ signiﬁcance obtained with the original DESY5 dataset. This preference necessitates the re-evaluation of phenomenological frameworks, including emergent dark energy models. The Phenomenologically Emergent Dark Energy (PEDE) model37 was later extended to the Generalized Emergent Dark Energy (GEDE) parameterization38 and subsequently to the Modiﬁed Emergent Dark Energy model39. In these models, the dark energy density is negligible in the early Universe, preserving the standard radiation- and matterdominated epochs, and increases only at late times to drive the observed cosmic acceleration. This emergent behavior is introduced to alleviate the coincidence problem while providing a testable framework for investigating the H0 and S8 tensions. Recently,40 introduced the Metastable Emergent Dark Energy (MEDE) model to describe late-time dark energy emergence and accommodate a smooth phantom-crossing (w = −1). Constrained by Planck CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and PantheonPlus data, the authors found a transition redshift of zt = 0.425+0.084 −0.120 and a variation amplitude of ∆= 0.87+0.29 −0.35. The MEDE framework demonstrates a statistically signiﬁ- cant deviation from a static cosmological constant; it is notably preferred over ΛCDM (∆DIC = −9.29) and performs comparably to the CPL parameterization, offering a highly competitive, dynamical alternative that preserves established early-universe physics. Another well-motivated extension of the standard cosmological model involves allowing a non-gravitational interaction between dark matter (DM) and dark energy (DE). Interacting dark energy (IDE) models have attracted considerable attention because they preserve the observational successes of the ΛCDM model while offering a possible mechanism to alleviate some of the existing cosmological tensions41–46. In these models, the energy exchange between the dark sector components is governed by an interaction term Q, usually parameterized through a dimensionless coupling parameter ξ. Such interactions can modify both the background expansion history and the growth of cosmic structures, providing a richer phenomenology than non-interacting dark energy models. This motivates extending the MEDE framework by incorporating a dark sector interaction, leading to the Interacting Metastable Emergent Dark Energy (IMEDE) model

investigated in this work. In the present work, we investigate the IMEDE framework through a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis using a combination of cosmological observations. Our dataset consists of Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) measurements from DESI DR2, Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) observations from Planck PR4 together with the Planck PR4 and ACT DR6 lensing likelihoods, and three Type Ia supernova compilations: Pantheon+, DES-Dovekie, and Union3. This combination enables robust constraints on the late-time expansion history while reducing parameter degeneracies. The primary objective of this work is to determine whether the IMEDE model can alleviate the H0 and S8 tensions while remaining consistent with current observational constraints. We further investigate whether introducing an interaction between dark matter and dark energy is supported by current cosmological observations and whether the IMEDE parameterization accommodates the dynamical phantom-crossing (Quintom-B) behavior indicated by the DESI DR2 background expansion data. Finally, through the evaluation of the interaction parameter Q together with the metastable dark energy parameters (zt and ∆), we quantify the statistical preference for the IMEDE model relative to the ΛCDM paradigm using Bayesian evidence. The paper is structured as follows: Section 1 presents the theoretical framework and mathematical formulation of the IMEDE model. Section 2 describes the observational datasets and the MCMC methodology used in this work. Section 3 presents the cosmological parameter constraints, investigates the implications for the H0 and S8 tensions, examines the statistical preference for an interaction between dark matter and dark energy, and discusses the evolution of the dark energy equation of state together with the overall cosmological implications of the IMEDE model. Finally, the main conclusions are summarized in Section 4.

## 1 Theoretical background

A possible interaction between dark matter and dark energy provides a well-motivated extension of the standard cosmological model. In the absence of a fundamental theory describing the dark sector, a phenomenological ﬂuid description is commonly adopted, in which dark matter (DM) and dark energy (DE) are treated as two interacting ﬂuids exchanging energy and momentum. Within this framework, the energy– momentum tensors of the two components are not conserved separately, but satisfy

∇µT µν (k) = Qν (k), (1)

where the index k denotes either DM or DE, and Qν (k) characterizes the energy–momentum exchange between the two sectors. The conservation of the total energy–momentum tensor, imposed by the Bianchi identities, requires Qν de = −Qν dm. In this work, we consider only energy exchange, Q0 de = −Q0 dm = Q, while the momentum transfer is assumed to vanish, i.e., Qi (k) = 0.

## 2 Dataset and Methodology

To constrain the parameters of the IMEDE model, we perform an MCMC analysis54–56 using the publicly available Bayesian cosmological parameter inference package Cobaya157. The convergence of the Markov chains is generated using the Gelman–Rubin statistic, requiring all chains to satisfy R − 1 < 0.01 before the sampling is considered converged58. The resulting posterior distributions are analyzed with the GetDist2 package59, while the theoretical predictions are computed with the Boltzmann solver Code for Anisotropies in the Microwave Background (CAMB)360,61. The baseline cosmological parameter vector is chosen as θ ΛCDM = {Ωcdm, Ωb, 100θMC, ln(1010As), ns, τ}. For the IMEDE model, this parameter space is extended by introducing the transition redshift zt, the transition width ∆, and the interaction coupling parameter Q, such that θ IMEDE = {θ ΛCDM, zt, ∆, Q}. Special care is taken in choosing the prior for the interaction parameter, Q.50 have shown that, in interacting dark energy models, the interaction parameter must have the opposite sign to (1+w) to avoid early-time gravitational instabilities. This point is particularly important because any successful solution of the H0 tension must also account for the value of the sound horizon at the drag epoch, rd. These two quantities are anti-correlated and can be regarded as two sides of the same coin. In general, if a cosmological model predicts a higher value of H0, closer to the local measurement reported by the SH0ES collaboration, (73.04±1.04),km,s−1,Mpc−180, it typically requires a corresponding reduction in rd of approximately 7%81. Indeed, this behavior can also be observed in the IMEDE model. Despite the different values of H0 inferred from the various dataset combinations, the corresponding values of rd remain essentially unchanged. This can be clearly seen in Table 2, where the constraints on H0 (Row 10) and rd (Row 14) show that the sound horizon at the drag epoch is nearly identical for all dataset combinations. Therefore, any dynamical dark energy model that aims to alleviate the H0 tension while leaving rd essentially unchanged is unlikely to provide a complete solution to the H0 tension82,83.

Yet, several attempts have been made to resolve the H0 tension by modifying the expansion history of the Universe around z ∼104 to z ∼10384. However, such modiﬁcations typically require a higher physical matter density, as is the case in Early Dark Energy (EDE) models. Although EDE provides a good ﬁt to the BAO + CMB observations and can reduce the H0 tension, it does not provide a satisfactory ﬁt to the SNe Ia datasets and also worsens the S8 tension85. We now discuss the main reason why the IMEDE model is unable to address the H0 tension. As mentioned earlier, the IMEDE model belongs to the class of interacting dynamical dark energy models and modiﬁes only the late-time expansion history of the Universe. In particular, the IMEDE model prefers an equation of state with w(z) > −1 at late times, a result that will be discussed in more detail in the following sections. As shown in 86–91, changing the dark energy equation of state from w(z) = −1 (ΛCDM) to w(z) > −1 (quintessence) generally leads to a lower inferred value of H0, whereas a phantom-like equation of state, w(z) < −1, typically favors a higher value of H0. For this reason, the IMEDE model is unable to resolve the H0 tension. This behavior is clearly reﬂected in our results, which give H0 = 65.2+1.2 −1.7, 67.46±0.59, 67.28±0.55, and 66.00± 0.81 kms−1 Mpc−1 for the CMB + DESI DR2, CMB + DESI DR2 + Pantheon+, CMB + DESI DR2 + DES-Dovekie, and CMB + DESI DR2 + Union3 dataset combinations, respectively. Quantitatively, the corresponding tensions with the SH0ES measurement are approximately 4.39σ, 4.67σ, 4.90σ, and 6.11σ, respectively. None of these values is consistent with the local SH0ES measurement, indicating that the IMEDE model does not alleviate the H0 tension. We also investigate the parameter S8 ≡σ8 (Ωm/0.3)0.5, which quantiﬁes the amplitude of matter density ﬂuctuations. The S8 tension is another important challenge in cosmology. Recent weak-lensing surveys, including the Dark Energy Survey (DES) Y6 (S8 = 0.794+0.009 −0.012)92, the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS)-Legacy (Shear) (S8 = 0.815+0.016 −0.021)16, and several others (see Table 1 of Ref.93), consistently favor lower values of S8 than the combined Planck + ACT + SPT constraint, S8 = 0.836+0.012 −0.013

92. In the IMEDE model, we obtain S8 = 0.892+0.032 −0.059, 0.834+0.010 −0.019, 0.8312+0.0090 −0.016 , and 0.839+0.012 −0.023 for the CMB + DESI DR2, CMB + DESI DR2 + Pantheon+, CMB + DESI DR2 + DES-Dovekie, and CMB + DESI DR2 + Union3 dataset combinations, respectively. Comparing these results with the KiDS-Legacy (Shear) weak-lensing measurement, the corresponding tensions are 1.75σ, 1.34σ, 1.45σ, and 1.66σ, respectively. Relative to the DES Y6 weak-lensing constraint, the corresponding tensions are 2.98σ, 2.63σ, 2.65σ, and 2.84σ, respectively. Although the inclusion of Type Ia supernova data reduces the S8 tension compared to the CMB + DESI DR2 dataset alone, the IMEDE model still predicts values of S8 that remain systematically higher than those preferred by current weak-lensing observations, particularly the DES Y6 results.

We now examine the constraints on the interaction parameter, Q, which determines both the strength and the direction of the energy exchange between dark matter and dark energy. In our model, negative values of Q (Q < 0) correspond to an energy transfer from dark matter to dark energy (DM →DE), whereas positive values (Q > 0) describe the opposite energy ﬂow (DE →DM). The standard noninteracting ΛCDM cosmology is recovered for Q = 0. Using the CMB+DESI DR2 dataset, we obtain only a lower bound on the interaction parameter, Q > −0.112 (95% C.L.), indicating no statistically signiﬁcant preference for a nonzero interaction. The inclusion of the Pantheon+, DES-Dovekie, and Union3 Type Ia supernova compilations yields similarly tight lower bounds, Q > −0.0980, Q > −0.111, and Q > −0.116, respectively. The consistent constraints obtained from the different Type Ia supernova compilations indicate that the current cosmological observations do not provide evidence for an interaction between dark matter and dark energy.

We now examine the constraints on the transition redshift, zt, obtained from the different dataset combinations. We ﬁnd zt = 0.431+0.12 −0.082, 0.316+0.092 −0.12 , 0.317+0.079 −0.098, and 0.398+0.079 −0.090 for the CMB + DESI DR2, CMB + DESI DR2 + Pantheon+, CMB + DESI DR2 + DES-Dovekie, and CMB + DESI DR2 + Union3 dataset combinations, respectively. Since w(zt) = −1, these results indicate that the phantom-divide crossing occurs at relatively low redshift, zt ≃0.3-0.4, during the late-time accelerated expansion of the Universe.

We also constrain the transition parameter ∆, obtaining ∆> 1.83, 1.06+0.37 −0.43, 1.28+0.39 −0.47, and 1.84 ± 0.51 for each dataset combination, respectively. The positive values of ∆indicate an evolution of the dark energy equation of state from a phantomlike phase (w < −1) at z > zt to a quintessence-like phase (w > −1) at z < zt. While the CMB + DESI DR2 dataset provides only a lower bound on ∆, the addition of the Type Ia supernova datasets yields tighter constraints on this parameter.

To assess the statistical preference for the IMEDE model relative to ΛCDM, we compare their best-ﬁt χ2 values obtained using IMINUIT94, deﬁning ∆χ2 MAP = χ2 IMEDE −χ2 ΛCDM. The IMEDE model extends ΛCDM through three additional parameters, Q, zt, and ∆. Under the assumptions of Gaussian likelihoods and a valid null hypothesis (ΛCDM), Wilks’ theorem95 implies that ∆χ2 MAP follows a χ2 distribution with one degree of freedom. The corresponding Gaussian signiﬁcance, Nσ, is then used to quantify the preference for the interacting dark sector model. We classify the preference as inconclusive (Nσ < 1), weak (1 ≤Nσ < 2.5), moderate (2.5 ≤Nσ < 5), strong (5 ≤Nσ < 10), or decisive (Nσ ≥10). A value of Nσ = 0 indicates that there is no statistical preference for the IMEDE model over ΛCDM, as the improvement in the best-ﬁt χ2 is either absent or too small to be statistically signiﬁcant.

The CMB + DESI DR2 and CMB + DESI DR2 + Pantheon+ dataset combinations yield ∆χ2 MAP = −9.30 and −9.00, corresponding to Gaussian signiﬁcances of Nσ = 2.23 and 2.18, respectively. According to our adopted classiﬁcation, these results provide weak statistical evidence in favor of the IMEDE model over ΛCDM. For the CMB + DESI DR2 + DES-Dovekie and CMB + DESI DR2 + Union3 dataset combinations, we obtain ∆χ2 MAP = −11.81 and −14.58, corresponding to Nσ = 2.65 and 3.06, respectively. These results indicate a moderate statistical preference for the IMEDE model over the standard ΛCDM cosmology.

The logarithmic Bayes factors are lnBIMEDE,ΛCDM = 7.89, 7.12, 9.01, and 10.33 for the CMB + DESI DR2, CMB + DESI DR2 + Pantheon+, CMB + DESI DR2 + DES-Dovekie, and CMB + DESI DR2 + Union3 dataset combinations, respectively. According to the revised Jeffreys’ scale, the ﬁrst three dataset combinations provide strong evidence in favor of the IMEDE model over ΛCDM, while the CMB + DESI DR2 + Union3 combination yields decisive evidence in favor of IMEDE model.

To further investigate the origin of the Bayesian preference for IDMDE, we compare the best-ﬁt predictions of the IDMDE and ΛCDM models with the DESI DR2 BAO distance measurements summarized in Table 3, while the corresponding residuals are shown in the upper panels of Fig. 3. A comparison across all four dataset combinations shows a stable pattern of residuals, indicating that the DESI BAO measurements largely drive the distance constraints, while the inclusion of Pantheon+, DES-Dovekie, or Union3 produces only minor shifts in the best-ﬁt predictions. Overall, both cosmological models provide a good description of the DESI DR2 BAO measurements. However, compared with ΛCDM, the IMEDE model systematically reduces the residuals for several BAO measurements, particularly those involving the radial distance zDH(z)/(rd √z) and the transverse comoving distance DM(z)/(rd √z). This improvement is observed consistently for all four dataset combinations and is not driven by a single BAO measurement. The largest improvement is found for the radial distance measurement zDH(z)/(rd √z) at z = 0.70. For the CMB + DESI DR2 dataset, the residual decreases from approximately 2.11σ in ΛCDM to 1.10σ in the IMEDE model. Similar improvements are found for the CMB + DESI DR2 + Pantheon+, CMB + DESI DR2 + DES-Dovekie, and CMB + DESI DR2 + Union3 combinations, where the residuals decrease from about 2.08–2.11σ in ΛCDM to approximately 1.48–1.99σ in the IMEDE model. Although this measurement remains the most discrepant BAO point, the tension is consistently reduced in the IMEDE scenario. A similarly signiﬁcant improvement is obtained for the radial distance measurement at z = 0.51. For the CMB + DESI DR2 combination, the residual decreases from 1.72σ in ΛCDM to only 0.46σ in the IMEDE model. Even after including the different Type Ia supernova compilations, the IMEDE residuals remain systematically smaller, ranging between 0.86σ and 1.43σ, whereas the corresponding ΛCDM residuals remain close to 1.7σ. Likewise, the transverse comoving distance measurements at z = 0.93 and z = 1.32 are reproduced substantially better by the IMEDE model, with residuals generally below 0.7σ, compared with values approaching or exceeding 1σ for ΛCDM. Several other BAO measurements are also reproduced slightly better by the IMEDE model. For example, the lowredshift volume-averaged distance DV(z)/(rd √z) at z = 0.29 shows a smaller residual for the CMB + DESI DR2 dataset, while the higher-redshift measurements of DV(z)/(rd √z) at z = 1.48 and DM(z)/(rd √z) at z = 2.33 are described at nearly the same level by both cosmological models. Overall, most of the remaining BAO measurements are reproduced within approximately the 1σ level by the IMEDE model. These results indicate that the statistical preference for the IMEDE model is not produced by a single outlying BAO measurement. Instead, it originates from a coherent reduction of the residuals across several independent DESI DR2 distance measurements spanning the full redshift range.

In Fig 4, we show the reconstructed evolution of H(z)/(1+ z) (ﬁrst row), q(z) (second row), w(z) (third row), and fDE(z) (fourth row) as functions of redshift for the IMEDE and ΛCDM models. In each panel, the solid curves denote the mean reconstructed evolution, whereas the darker and lighter shaded regions correspond to the 1σ and 2σ conﬁdence intervals, respectively. The ﬁrst row compares the evolution of H(z)/(1 + z) predicted by the IMEDE and ΛCDM models. For the CMB + DESI DR2 dataset, the IMEDE model predicts values that are slightly lower than those of the ΛCDM model over the intermediate redshift range. After including the Pantheon+, DES-Dovekie, and Union3 supernova samples, the predictions of the two models become similar, with only small residual differences that are most clearly visible in the zoom-in panels. The second row shows the evolution of the deceleration parameter, q(z), for the IMEDE and ΛCDM models. Both models show the transition from a decelerating (q > 0) to an accelerating (q < 0) Universe. Compared to ΛCDM, the IMEDE model predicts a slightly less negative deceleration parameter at low redshift, indicating a marginally weaker present-day acceleration. The third row presents the reconstructed evolution of the dark energy equation of state, w(z), for the IMEDE model, while the ΛCDM model corresponds to the constant value w = −1. For all four dataset combinations, the reconstructed equation of state exhibits a transition from the phantom regime (w < −1) at low redshift to the quintessence regime (w > −1) at higher redshift, crossing the phantom divide, w = −1, at z ∼0.3–0.5. This behavior is characteristic of a Quintom-B dark energy scenario35. The fourth row shows the corresponding evolution of the normalized dark energy density, fDE(z). While the ΛCDM model predicts a constant value, fDE(z) = 1, the IMEDE model satisﬁes fDE(0) = 1 at the present epoch for all dataset combinations. As the redshift increases, fDE(z) initially shows a mild enhancement above unity before decreasing below the ΛCDM prediction, reﬂecting the dynamical evolution of dark energy in the IMEDE model.

## 4 Conclusions

In this work, we have presented a comprehensive observational study of the Interacting Metastable Emergent Dark Energy model using the DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation measurements combined with Planck PR4 CMB observations and three different Type Ia supernova catalog. Our primary objective was to investigate whether current cosmological observations support an interacting metastable emergent dark energy scenario and to examine the preference of the interaction between dark matter and dark energy. Our statistical analysis consistently favors the IMEDE model over the standard ΛCDM cosmology for all dataset combinations considered. Based on the Gaussian signiﬁcance, the CMB + DESI DR2 and CMB + DESI DR2 + Pantheon+ combinations provide weak statistical evidence in favor of the IMEDE model, while the CMB + DESI DR2 + DES-

Dovekie and CMB + DESI DR2 + Union3 combinations yield a moderate statistical preference. Bayesian model comparison further strengthens this result, providing strong evidence for the IMEDE model for the ﬁrst three dataset combinations and decisive evidence for the CMB + DESI DR2 + Union3 combination. The statistical preference for the IMEDE model is not driven by a single anomalous BAO measurement. Instead, it originates from a coherent reduction of the residuals across several independent DESI DR2 distance measurements spanning the full observed redshift range. In particular, the largest improvements occur for the radial BAO measurements at z = 0.51 and z = 0.70, together with noticeable improvements in several transverse distance measurements. These results indicate that the IMEDE model provides a more consistent description of the DESI DR2 distance measurements than the standard ΛCDM cosmology. The reconstructed expansion history also reveals several distinctive features of the IMEDE scenario. The dark energy equation of state undergoes a transition from a phantom phase at earlier times to a quintessence phase at recent epochs, crossing the phantom divide at z ≃0.3–0.5. This Quintom-B behavior naturally emerges from the Interacting Metastable Emergent Dark Energy framework and is accompanied by a smooth evolution of the dark energy density without introducing any signiﬁcant modiﬁcation to the early-Universe physics. Despite these encouraging results, the IMEDE model does not provide a complete solution to either the H0 or the S8 tensions. Since the IMEDE modiﬁes only the late-time evolution of the Universe, the sound horizon at the drag epoch remains essentially unchanged. Consequently, although the inferred values of the Hubble constant vary among the different dataset combinations, they remain signiﬁcantly lower than the SH0ES determination. Likewise, the predicted values of S8 remain systematically higher than those preferred by current weak-lensing surveys, particularly DES Y6. Overall, our results demonstrate that the IMEDE model provides a statistically well-motivated extension of the standard cosmological model and offers a good description of the DESI DR2 observations. The emergence of a Quintom-B dark energy evolution together with the coherent improvement across multiple independent BAO measurements suggests that the observed preference is unlikely to arise from a single statistical ﬂuctuation. If conﬁrmed by forthcoming DESI DR3 observations and future surveys such as Euclid, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, these results could provide important evidence for a dynamical and interacting dark sector beyond the standard ΛCDM paradigm.
